summary: Specifies the Licklider Transmission Protocol, designed to give retransmission-based reliability over links with very long round-trip times or frequent interruptions, such as deep space links. It is aimed at long-haul reliable transmission and is published as an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Imagine mailing long messages to a space station: you must remember what you sent in case a piece gets lost. This describes how to resend only the missing pieces across very long delays.

questions: what is ltp licklider transmission protocol
what are red and green parts in ltp
subtitle: Reliable delivery for links with huge delays and frequent outages, such as deep space.

tldr.problem: On links with extremely long round-trip times or frequent interruptions, handshakes and per-packet conversations take far too long.
tldr.mechanism: LTP sends a block as data segments, marks checkpoints, and has the receiver answer with reports of what arrived so that only the missing parts are resent. It has no negotiation or handshakes.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol from the Delay Tolerant Networking Research Group. It has no flow or congestion control, so it is not meant for the global Internet.

today: RFC 5326 is an Experimental RFC from the Delay Tolerant Networking Research Group, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says it may be considered for standardization by the IETF in the future, which the IETF note disclaims any view on.

sections.title: What LTP Is For
sections.content:
The Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) provides retransmission-based reliability over links with extremely long round-trip times, frequent interruptions, or both. Interplanetary communication is the main example. LTP does Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) by asking for selective-acknowledgment reception reports. It is stateful and has no negotiation or handshakes.

In the Interplanetary Internet setting, LTP is meant to be a reliable "convergence layer" under the Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050), working between adjacent nodes in direct radio contact. It usually runs directly over a data-link layer, which must ensure data integrity. The motivation is in RFC 5325 and the security extensions are in RFC 5327.

LTP has no flow control or congestion control, so it is not intended or appropriate for ubiquitous deployment in the global Internet. Over UDP it must only be used for software development or in private local area networks. The RFC carries an IESG note saying it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.
sections.eli5: It is a way to send data reliably when messages take so long to travel that waiting for a reply to every packet would be silly. It is only for special links, not the whole Internet.

sections.title: Blocks, Red and Green Parts, and Sessions
sections.content:
The client service (usually the Bundle Protocol) hands LTP a block, an array of contiguous octets. The first part of the block, the red-part, is sent reliably with acknowledgment and retransmission. The rest, the green-part, is sent unreliably. A block may be all red, and the red-part length can be anything from zero to the full block length.

A session is one thread of LTP activity between two peer engines to transmit one block. Data flows one way, from sender to receiver, while acknowledgments flow back. Each engine has an engine ID, and a session ID is made of the originator's engine ID plus a session number, which is typically random for anti-DoS reasons.

The unit sent is a segment. A checkpoint is a data segment that asks the receiver for a reception report, which lists which octet ranges (reception claims) have arrived. The last red segment is the end of red-part (EORP), and the last segment of the block is the end of block (EOB). Numbers in the headers use SDNV encoding: the top bit of each octet says whether more octets follow, and the other 7 bits carry value.
sections.eli5: The first part of your message is sent with a promise to fix any losses, and the last part is just tossed out and hoped for. A checkpoint is the sender asking, what have you got so far?

sections.title: Segment Format
sections.content:
Every segment has a header, zero or more octets of content and an optional trailer. The header starts with a control byte: a 4-bit version number (0000 for this version) and 4 segment type flags named CTRL, EXC, Flag 1 and Flag 0. After that come the session ID and an extensions count octet. The high 4 bits give the number of extension TLVs in the header, the low 4 bits the number in the trailer, so each can hold 0 to 15 extensions.

The flags give 16 segment type codes. Data segments (CTRL 0) are red when EXC is 0 and green when EXC is 1. Control segments are report segments, report-acknowledgments, and cancel segments with their acknowledgments, separately for the block sender and the block receiver.

A data segment carries a client service ID (like a TCP port number), an offset, a length and the data. Checkpoints also carry a checkpoint serial number and a report serial number. A report segment carries a report serial number, the checkpoint serial number it answers, an upper bound and a lower bound, and a list of reception claims. Serial numbers MUST NOT be zero, and the first of each is chosen randomly for security.
sections.eli5: Each piece has a label that says what kind of piece it is, which message it belongs to, and where in the message it goes. Special pieces are used for asking questions and for answers.

sections.title: How Retransmission and Cancellation Work
sections.content:
The sender splits the block into segments, flags the last red one as a checkpoint and EORP, and the last segment overall as EOB. It starts a timer when a checkpoint is sent. The receiver answers a checkpoint with a report segment (RS), and the sender acknowledges that with a report-acknowledgment (RA). If the report shows gaps, the sender resends the missing data, marking the last resent segment as a new checkpoint. When the whole red-part is known to be received, the session closes.

Timers account for the one-way light time plus extra anticipated latency, which the RFC suggests could default to 2 seconds. Timers are suspended while the peer is known not to be transmitting. Retransmission is limited by values set by network management; exceeding them cancels the session with reason code RLEXC.

Either side can cancel a session with a cancel segment carrying a one-byte reason code, which the peer acknowledges. Reception reports are binding: a receiver may not renege on data it has claimed.
sections.eli5: The sender asks which pieces arrived, the receiver lists them, and the sender resends only the missing ones. If it keeps failing, either side can say stop, and the other one confirms.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists denial-of-service risks: a fake cancel segment can bring down a session, deleted or corrupted acknowledgments can make timers expire, and an attacker can flood an engine or fill its storage. Anti-DoS measures include partly random session numbers, random starting serial numbers, frequent checkpoints or asynchronous reports to detect trouble sooner, and the authentication extension in RFC 5327.

It gives a sample replay-handling algorithm using a cache of segment hashes and stored pre-cooked responses. Implementations SHOULD sanity-check SDNV lengths, MUST check that offsets and lengths are consistent, and MUST use sufficiently long random values.
sections.eli5: Bad guys could send fake messages or flood the receiver. Using random numbers and checking everything carefully makes that harder.
